title: CLAIRMONT: Officer of SIU probe has heavy burden
article: After the uniformed Hamilton police officer shot and killed a man downtown Friday night, he was stripped of his gun and put in a room by himself.
He was kept there - separated from his colleagues - while he completed his notes.

That process is designed to collect evidence and maintain the integrity of the Special Investigations Unit's probe into the incident. But it also cuts the officer off from his entire support system when he needs it most.

"You've had an officer involved in a traumatic event and they are segregated and isolated," says Clint Twolan, president of the Hamilton Police Association (HPA). "In a critical incident, in many cases people have been traumatized."

Twolan cannot speak specifically about this "officer involved shooting" due to an automatic gag order that comes with an SIU investigation. It invokes its mandate any time there is a death, serious injury or allegation of sexual assault involving a police officer.

Tony Divers, 36, was killed after being shot just before midnight Friday on James Street South. The SIU says he was walking in the middle of the street, near the GO station and that there were "reports" he had a gun.
The officer was in uniform and arrived in a marked cruiser, according to Twolan. A cab driver and a pedestrian saw some of the exchange unfold.
The SIU has said the officer fired more than once.

Just minutes before that, Divers assaulted his estranged wife, Madeleine Divers, outside the Dirty Dog Saloon on King William Street where she is a security guard. A security video shows him hitting her.
She says he was mentally unwell, on drugs, and he needed help.
She says she reported the assault to police and told them her husband did not have a gun at the time.
Divers had a history of violence. He was convicted of manslaughter in a 2002 homicide, and had convictions for assault with a weapon and domestic violence.
Immediately after the shooting the "subject officer" was taken from the scene to a police station, says Twolan.
His gun and other "use of force" equipment - baton, Taser - were seized. His boots and other clothing may have been taken too.
"Anything that can be evidence is taken," explains Twolan. "Are you going to find gunshot residue? Blood spatter?"

Next, it was determined if the officer needed medical care, either for any physical injuries or mental health concerns. (If he had been seriously injured during the incident he would have received care immediately.)

The officer was then assigned a "buddy," another Hamilton police officer who is not involved in the shooting. The buddy can have contact with the subject officer to "monitor" him to be sure he is safe, bring him a cup of coffee or offer to call his family, but cannot speak to him about the incident.
Twolan says the Hamilton Police Service takes good care of its officers after a critical incident involving the SIU.

It is mandatory for the subject officer to complete his notes "without speaking to anybody," says Twolan. He then hands them over to a Hamilton officer who is the designated "liaison" with the SIU. Only then can the subject officer have contact with the HPA which usually has a criminal lawyer lined up for the officer by then.
"It is a criminal investigation," says Twolan.
The lawyer will advise the officer on whether he should permit the liaison to turn his notes over to the SIU. A subject officer has the legal right not to share his notes.
In the most minor SIU matters, it is possible the subject officer will resume his duties later that same shift.

That was not the case Friday. That officer was taken home. It is at the discretion of Chief Eric Girt as to when the officer is eligible to return to work and whether they will be back on the road or on the desk. Twolan says the association generally encourages officers to get back to the job as soon as possible.
Meanwhile, the SIU investigation is ongoing. So is the media coverage and social media speculation.
"It's frustrating that we're muzzled from talking," says Twolan. "The speculation hurts the officer psychologically and emotionally. You know the truth, but you can't defend yourself."
Twolan will say this: "I'm confident that when all of the details come in, the officer's response was in line with the training he received."
It can take weeks, if not months for the SIU to complete an investigation like this.

"I can't stress enough the trauma that is involved for the officer," says Twolan. "Police come to work every day to save lives - not to take them. This officer will live with this for the rest of his life."
